text: Churn prediction is the classic applied classification project: which customers are likely to leave, so the business can reach out first? Before writing code, write one sentence. Each month, rank active customers by churn risk so the retention team can contact the riskiest twenty percent. That sentence names the target, the metric, and the action.

On four thousand illustrative customers, the overall churn rate is twenty-seven point two percent. Month-to-month customers churn at thirty-six point four percent, versus just ten point four percent on two-year contracts. That gap is an early hint of what the model should find.

Hold out twenty percent as a test set first, then compare candidates with cross-validation on training data only. A dummy baseline sits at point five, pure chance. Plain logistic regression scores point eight oh six AUC. A two-hundred-tree random forest scores point seven eight two, actually worse. Here the true signal is close to linear, so complexity doesn't pay off.

Touch the test set exactly once, with logistic regression. Test AUC comes in at point eight oh two, right in line with cross-validation, no sign of overfitting the selection. But at the default point five threshold, recall for churners is only point four four seven. A plain yes or no cutoff would miss most of them.

Turn scores into a call list instead. Rank everyone by predicted risk and contact the riskiest twenty percent, one hundred sixty customers. Sixty-four point four percent of that group actually churns, against a twenty-seven point one percent base rate, and it captures forty-seven point five percent of every churner in the test set.

Permutation importance shuffles one input at a time and measures how far the score falls. Tenure and contract type dominate; autopay matters least. That ranking is what turns a probability into an explanation the business can act on.
Frame the action and metric first, baseline before modeling, touch the test set once, then translate scores into a ranked list. Next: the same workflow applied to price prediction.
